prompt_free_text:
This paper studies motion forecasting under a “continuous driving” setting rather than the standard one-shot benchmark formulation. The core idea is intuitive and practically motivated: successive forecasting calls in an autonomous driving stack are temporally related, so a predictor should exploit prior scene context and prior predictions instead of treating each scene independently. To this end, the paper proposes RealMotion, which combines a scene context stream that propagates encoded scene features across time and an agent trajectory stream that stores and reuses prior predicted trajectories through a memory bank and refinement module. The paper also introduces a data reorganization procedure that converts existing benchmark scenes into short temporal sequences to emulate continuous driving. Empirically, the method reports strong results on Argoverse 2 and Argoverse 1, including leaderboard-level numbers and favorable latency/parameter tradeoffs.

Overall, I find the paper interesting and potentially impactful. The problem framing is valuable: the mismatch between benchmark evaluation and real deployment is real, and the paper makes a credible case that repeated forecasting should be modeled as a sequential process. The proposed architecture is also reasonably simple and modular, which is a strength. The empirical results are strong, and the ablations suggest that both temporal streams contribute. At the same time, I have several concerns about the exact novelty relative to prior temporal/streaming forecasting work, the fairness and interpretation of the benchmark adaptation, and some missing methodological details that make it difficult to fully assess the contribution and reproducibility.

The strongest aspect of the paper is the problem formulation. Many forecasting papers optimize a single prediction from a fixed observation window, whereas real systems repeatedly re-plan and re-predict. The paper’s emphasis on exploiting temporal continuity across successive forecasting calls is well motivated, and the qualitative example about currently invisible agents or evolving intent is compelling. I also appreciate that the method is not excessively complicated: the scene context stream uses cross-attention over aligned historical scene features, and the trajectory stream uses a memory bank of prior predictions to refine current outputs. This decomposition is conceptually clean and easy to understand.

The empirical section is also a strength. On Argoverse 2 single-agent forecasting, the reported gains over the independent variant are substantial, especially for single-mode metrics, and the method appears competitive with or better than strong baselines such as QCNet. The ablation table is useful in showing incremental gains from data reorganization, scene-context propagation, and trajectory relaying. The efficiency table is also encouraging: the model is small and online latency is reasonable. If these numbers hold under a fair deployment setting, this would be a meaningful practical contribution.

That said, my main concern is that a significant fraction of the gains may come from changing the task/data formulation rather than from the model itself, and the paper does not fully disentangle these effects. The proposed “data reorganization” creates multiple sub-scenes from a single benchmark sample by splitting along historical frames and then training/evaluating sequentially. This is central to the paper, but it also changes the effective supervision structure and potentially the information available to the model across steps. While the authors compare against a non-sequential variant RealMotion-I, they do not provide sufficiently strong adapted baselines. For example, the fairest comparison would be to take several strong existing methods and train/evaluate them under the same reorganized sequential protocol, perhaps with simple temporal aggregation or memory added, to determine whether the gains are due to the specific RealMotion design or simply due to exposing the model to multiple overlapping sub-scenes and repeated refinement opportunities. The text mentions adapting QCNet in the appendix, but this is not visible in the main paper and seems too important to relegate. Without stronger baseline adaptation, it is hard to know whether the paper demonstrates a new modeling advance or mostly a new benchmark protocol plus a competent architecture.

Relatedly, the evaluation protocol needs to be clarified much more carefully. The paper distinguishes “offline” and “online” latency and notes that only the final prediction is used for evaluation in the offline dataset setting, whereas each iteration is meaningful online. This raises an important question: when reporting benchmark metrics, is the model effectively allowed to make several forecasting passes as time advances and then only the last one is scored? If so, this is not directly comparable to standard one-shot methods that must predict the full horizon from a single observation endpoint. In other words, the method may be benefiting from additional elapsed time before the final scored prediction. The paper should explicitly state, for each benchmark result, what observation history is available at each scored step and whether the final evaluated prediction corresponds to a later timestamp than in the original benchmark. Figure 4 suggests predictions at 3s, 4s, and 5s with the final one used for evaluation, which could imply that the model has seen more recent observations than standard methods before producing the scored forecast. If that interpretation is correct, the comparison to standard leaderboard methods is not apples-to-apples. This is the single most important issue that needs clarification.

Even if the reorganized protocol preserves the original final prediction horizon in some transformed way, the paper should formalize it precisely. A timeline diagram with original observation/prediction windows and reorganized sub-scene windows would help substantially. The current description is too ambiguous, especially around “extending from split points both into the past and the future,” “same prediction horizon as the original,” and “the number of historical and future steps is determined by the minimum split point and the length of ground-truth trajectory.” It is difficult to reconstruct exactly what data each sub-scene contains and how labels are assigned.

On novelty, the paper’s framing is fresh, but the technical contribution feels somewhat incremental. The scene context stream is essentially temporal cross-attention over aligned scene features, and the trajectory stream is a memory-based refinement mechanism over prior predictions. These are sensible designs, but they are not conceptually far from existing temporal modeling, recurrent memory, or historical prediction refinement ideas. The paper cites streaming motion forecasting and some temporal modeling work, but the distinction from these lines is not sharply articulated. In particular, the paper should better explain how it differs from prior work that uses historical predictions, recurrent scene encodings, or streaming benchmarks. Is the main novelty the benchmark reorganization, the dual-stream architecture, or the combination? Right now the contribution statement somewhat overclaims a “fundamental limitation” in prior work without sufficiently positioning the method against the closest temporal/streaming approaches.

I also have some methodological questions. First, the scene context stream propagates map features across time via map-map attention after alignment. Since HD maps are static in global coordinates, it is not obvious why temporal propagation of map embeddings is necessary beyond coordinate transformation and re-encoding. The paper argues that local map sampling differs across sub-scenes, which is fair, but then the benefit may come from enlarging effective map coverage rather than temporal reasoning per se. This should be discussed more explicitly. Second, the agent trajectory stream stores predicted trajectories rather than ground-truth histories. This is realistic for deployment, but it introduces error accumulation risk. The paper does not analyze failure modes when early predictions are poor, nor does it compare against using encoded observed trajectories only. Third, the memory bank design is underspecified: how many trajectories are stored, how are they retrieved, are all modes from all prior steps used, what is the computational complexity as the bank grows, and how sensitive is performance to bank size? These details matter for both reproducibility and understanding.

The training description is also somewhat thin. The paper says gradients are computed for all segments to “fully utilize historical information,” but it is unclear whether backpropagation is truncated through time across the sequence, whether the memory bank is differentiable across segments, and whether teacher forcing or detached states are used. Similarly, the auxiliary singular trajectory prediction for other agents is mentioned but not described in enough detail to reproduce. The loss weighting is fixed to equal weights without justification; some sensitivity analysis would be useful.

The ablations are helpful but still incomplete. The component ablation shows that data reorganization alone already yields a sizable gain, which reinforces my earlier concern that the protocol change itself is a major factor. This makes it even more important to compare against stronger baselines under the same protocol. I would also like to see ablations on memory bank size, number of stored modes, whether using ground-truth past trajectories instead of predicted ones changes results, and robustness under longer sequences. Since the paper’s central claim is about continuous driving, experiments on sequence length and degradation over time would be especially informative. For example, how does performance evolve over 10, 20, or more successive forecasting steps? Does the context stream saturate or drift? Does the trajectory memory help more in dense interactive scenes than in simple lane-following scenes?

Another concern is the use of leaderboard comparisons. Several compared methods use ensembles while others do not, and some numbers are from different settings. That is acceptable if clearly marked, but because the proposed method also changes the evaluation protocol, the leaderboard comparison should be interpreted cautiously. I would strongly prefer a controlled validation-set comparison where all methods are run under the same reorganized setting and same observation budget. The current presentation risks overstating state-of-the-art status.

The writing is understandable overall, but there are many grammatical issues and several places where the exposition is imprecise. Some examples include inconsistent terminology around “continuous,” “online,” and “offline”; unclear notation in Eq. (3), especially the origin selection via y_i[Δt·q]; and vague statements such as “modifying initial predictions using the memory bank proves more effective” without evidence. The paper would benefit from careful editing and a more rigorous description of the protocol.

Despite these concerns, I think the paper has real merit. The practical motivation is strong, the architecture is plausible, and the empirical gains are promising. My recommendation depends heavily on whether the evaluation is truly comparable to standard forecasting benchmarks. If the final scored prediction uses more recent observations than competing methods, then the headline results are not directly comparable and the paper’s claims should be substantially toned down. If, however, the authors can clearly demonstrate that the reorganized protocol preserves the same information budget and that strong baselines under the same protocol do not obtain similar gains, then this would be a valuable contribution.

For improvement, I would suggest the following. First, add a precise formal definition of the continuous-driving task and the data reorganization procedure, ideally with a timeline figure and pseudocode. Second, provide controlled comparisons against at least one or two strong baselines retrained under the same reorganized sequential setting. Third, clarify exactly what information is available at each prediction step and why the benchmark comparison is fair. Fourth, expand the ablations to include memory bank size, retrieval strategy, sequence length, and error accumulation analysis. Fifth, discuss more carefully the relation to prior streaming/temporal forecasting work and moderate novelty claims where appropriate.

In summary, this is an interesting and practically motivated paper with strong empirical promise, but there are important concerns about evaluation fairness, protocol clarity, and the extent to which gains stem from the new task formulation versus the proposed model. I lean positive on the idea, but I would want these issues addressed before fully endorsing the paper.

prompt_structured_json.summary: This paper studies motion forecasting under a continuous driving setting rather than treating each scene independently. It proposes RealMotion, which augments a standard encoder-decoder predictor with two temporal mechanisms: a scene context stream that propagates historical scene features across successive sub-scenes via cross-attention, and an agent trajectory stream that stores past predicted trajectories/features in a memory bank and refines current predictions using trajectory-conditioned attention. To enable training on standard benchmarks, the paper reorganizes Argoverse scenes into short continuous sub-scene sequences by splitting trajectories at multiple historical timestamps. Experiments on Argoverse 1 and 2 report strong leaderboard results, favorable ablations, and competitive inference latency.
strengths: Addresses an important and underexplored mismatch between benchmark evaluation and real deployment: forecasting is repeatedly executed over time, not as isolated one-shot predictions.
The proposed formulation is intuitive and practically motivated, combining temporal scene-context propagation and trajectory-memory-based refinement in a modular way.
Empirical results on Argoverse 2 single-agent and multi-agent leaderboards are strong, with clear gains over the paper's independent baseline and competitive or state-of-the-art benchmark numbers.

Ablation studies cover the main components (data reorganization, scene context stream, agent trajectory stream, alignment, trajectory embedding, depth, split points), which helps support the contribution claims.
The method appears parameter-efficient relative to several strong baselines, and the paper explicitly discusses online vs offline latency.
weaknesses: The central novelty partly depends on a benchmark-specific data reorganization procedure rather than a cleanly defined continuous-driving dataset/protocol; this makes it harder to assess whether gains reflect better forecasting or favorable sample construction.

The comparison to prior methods is not fully controlled: many baseline numbers come from leaderboards with different backbones, training recipes, and in some cases ensembles, while the paper's own baseline RealMotion-I is much weaker than the strongest prior art, making attribution of gains less clear.

The methodology is underspecified in several important places, including memory-bank retrieval/update details, how agents are associated across sub-scenes, how many trajectories/features are retrieved, and how training/inference differ under the sequential setup.

The paper claims improved real-world efficiency, but the reported offline latency for RealMotion is substantially higher than the independent variant, and the online latency argument relies on an application interpretation rather than a directly comparable benchmark protocol.
The writing occasionally overstates conclusions (e.g., 'conclusively demonstrates', 'far outperformed') despite relatively modest gains on some metrics and limited evidence beyond Argoverse.

There is limited analysis of robustness issues such as error accumulation from feeding past predictions into future refinement, sensitivity to memory-bank size, or failure cases where historical predictions are wrong.
methodological_flaws: The empirical protocol may introduce train/test mismatch and possible information leakage concerns through data reorganization. Splitting a single annotated scene into multiple overlapping sub-scenes creates highly correlated samples; the paper does not rigorously analyze whether this inflates effective sample size or makes optimization/evaluation easier in a way not comparable to standard one-shot baselines.

The scientific claim that existing methods 'totally ignore' temporal relationships across successive scenes is overstated; some prior work already studies temporal/streaming forecasting, and the paper does not provide a sufficiently careful controlled comparison against such methods under the same protocol.

Equation (3) for trajectory alignment is not fully well-defined. The transform uses the current heading angle and an origin indexed by y_i[Δt·q], but the sign convention, reference frame, and handling of non-integer or out-of-range indices are unspecified. This makes the geometric correctness of the alignment unclear.

The scene-context alignment via MLN in Eq. (1) is presented as if it projects historical scene features into the current coordinate system, but MLN is a feature modulation mechanism, not an explicit geometric transform. This weakens the logical justification that the features are truly aligned across time.

The agent trajectory stream refines current predictions using past predicted trajectories rather than ground-truth histories, which can cause compounding errors. The paper does not provide a causal analysis, oracle study, or robustness experiment to validate that the memory bank helps when historical predictions are imperfect.

Loss design is simplistic and insufficiently justified. Using equal weights for regression, classification, and refinement losses is arbitrary, and there is no sensitivity analysis. Since refinement depends on initial predictions, optimization interactions could materially affect results.

The efficiency comparison is not fully apples-to-apples. RealMotion's 'online' latency is compared to HPTR online, but benchmark metrics are reported for offline evaluation; meanwhile RealMotion offline requires multiple iterations. This weakens the empirical validity of the efficiency claim for standard benchmark usage.
